chunks: And the blood money (diyah) of the shoulder, when the shoulder bone is broken, is one-fifth of the blood money of the hand, which is one hundred dinars. So if there is a crack in the shoulder, its blood money is four-fifths of the blood money for its breaking, which is eighty dinars. So if it is exposed, its blood money is one-quarter of the blood money for its breaking, which is twenty-five dinars. So if the bones are displaced from it, its blood money is one hundred and seventy-five dinars: of which one hundred dinars is for its complete breaking, and fifty dinars for the displacement of its bones, and twenty-five dinars for its exposure. So if it is pierced, its blood money is one-quarter of the blood money for its breaking, which is twenty-five dinars. So if it is bruised and becomes defective, its blood money is one-third of the blood money of the soul, which is three hundred and thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar. So if it is disjointed, its blood money is thirty dinars.

key_terms.دِيَة: Blood money / financial compensation for injury or death
key_terms.نَاقِبَة: Piercing (a deep wound penetrating the bone)

ai.seo_question: What is the blood money (diyah) for a broken or injured shoulder in Shia Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi provides a detailed jurisprudential breakdown of *diyah* (blood money) for shoulder injuries, reflecting the classical Shia legal tradition's precision in categorizing injuries by severity and functional impact. It illustrates the methodological approach of early scholars like al-Kulayni in deriving specific monetary values from proportional fractions of the full *diyah*, ensuring equitable compensation for physical harm.
